source.title: The Efficiency Gap in Byte Modeling
source.authors: Celine Lee; J. Yan; Chen Liang; Jia-Xin Shi; Yin Zhang; Jeremiah Liu; Peng-Cheng Yin; F. Pereira; E. Chi; Zhiyuan Cheng; Alexander M. Rush; Ruoxi Wang

record.file_problem: The text is substantially complete, including appendices, but one extracted page (around page 6) contains severe OCR corruption. It does not appear to remove the reported scaling or downstream results.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out BPB over compute and model-size sweeps, using a compute-matched scaling setup that differs from the original scaling-law studies and includes byte and BPE representations and AR and masked-diffusion objectives.
record.gate_note: The paper reports extrapolated parity budgets, but does not train runs at those budgets to validate the forecasts; V2 is therefore not tested. It does not report compute-optimal parameter/token growth laws or architecture-shape comparisons. Entropy-boundary analysis, permutation experiments, and span-masking results concern mechanisms or interventions rather than the claim versions and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs a Chinchilla-style isoFLOP sweep (48M–1.23B params, 6e18–2e21 FLOPs) of held-out BPB in new settings (byte vs BPE, AR vs masked diffusion). It fits power laws to isoFLOP minima, and to the byte/BPE ratio, against compute. It also gives zero-shot benchmarks at two model sizes.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the byte-modeling compute penalty depends on objective: AR byte models approach BPE parity at scale (extrapolated ~1e22 FLOPs), while byte MDMs keep a large offset (parity extrapolated ~4e26). They hypothesize context fragility, supported by permutation experiments, and call for structural adaptations for byte-level diffusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a compute-matched sweep and held-out BPB, but studies byte versus BPE representations and AR versus masked diffusion, and uses BPB rather than the original studies’ loss setup. The paper describes its protocol as following Hoffmann et al. (2022).
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling overhead changes with modeling objective (AR versus MDM) and representation (byte versus BPE). The paper also reports vocabulary-size and compute-budget dependence in its appendix, but does not provide those as tests of the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal BPE vocabulary size for MDM shifts with model size and compute: Llama-2 is best at 180M, while GPT-2 and Llama-3 overtake it at 717M around 1e20 FLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal tokenizer vocabulary size grows with compute budget.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed outcomes. The downstream evaluation covers selected model pairs and simple benchmarks; the authors say HumanEval, MBPP, and BBH performance was near-zero or random chance and omit those numbers. The largest-budget parity statements are extrapolations rather than evaluated runs. One extracted page is garbled.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted to meet the cap. Mechanistic entropy, permutation, compressibility, and span-masking outcomes are not scaling-law or downstream-predictability results as defined by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No separate power laws in parameters or tokens. The compute range is only ~2.5 orders of magnitude.
Parity budgets (1.3e22, 4.2e26 FLOPs) are extrapolations never validated by larger runs.
IsoFLOP optima are plotted, but no N_opt or D_opt exponents versus compute are reported.
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. Byte and MDM runs remain text pretraining.
Only two model sizes are compared. There is no fitted downstream-vs-scale or downstream-vs-loss relation.

missing.what: Power-law fit of isoFLOP minimum BPB vs FLOPs per configuration; exponents and fit quality not stated.
Loss-minimising parameter count per compute budget, from the isoFLOP parabolas, for each configuration.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T3: Chinchilla isoFLOP protocol applied to byte and MDM settings. V5 links removed because byte and MDM runs are text LM pretraining. D1–D32 are single-size points that serve only as baselines for the D33–D48 scale comparison. The 717M capacity-match models use more compute than the 180M compute-match models, so the scale increase confounds params and compute. No uncertainty is reported anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: Does not separately fit or establish loss exponents for parameter count and token count; tests compute-related BPB trajectories over the reported model and compute sweeps.
No extrapolated larger run is evaluated against the fit; reported parity budgets are forecasts, not validation.
Does not report how compute-optimal parameter count and token count each scale with compute.
Uses a standard Transformer setup rather than varying depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests AR versus masked-diffusion objectives for text pretraining, but not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports selected zero-shot reasoning benchmarks for compute-matched and capacity-matched models, not a broad downstream scaling curve or a systematic relation to pretraining loss.
Does not investigate sensitivity of exponents or compute-optimal allocation to parameter counting, schedules, data, or fitting choices, or compare published scaling-law fits.

rows.subject: AR byte model sweep
rows.operation_detail: Compute-matched sweep; BPB plotted against training FLOPs and compared with AR BPE models.

conditions.value: F ∈ {6e18, 2e19, 6e20, 2e21} and additional budgets shown in the paper

rows.value: The gap narrows with compute; byte models initially lag, and trajectories begin to converge as they approach the 1e22 FLOPs regime. The paper says the models approach performance parity at scale.
rows.note: The report describes a sweep/family, not a single checkpoint. Parity at approximately 1.3e22 FLOPs is an extrapolation, not an evaluated run.
rows.check: V1 concerns BPB falling with compute, which it does for AR byte and AR BPE (Fig 1–3). Linking to V5 is wrong: this is still text LM pretraining. The byte–BPE gap is not the V1 effect, so the state is observed, not partial.

rows.subject: MDM byte model sweep
rows.operation_detail: Compute-matched sweep; BPB plotted against training FLOPs and compared with MDM BPE models.

conditions.value: F ∈ {6e18, 2e19, 6e20, 2e21} and additional budgets shown in the paper

rows.value: Byte MDM shows a downward learning trajectory but retains a substantial performance offset across the studied scales; the text describes a longer-sustained offset than for AR.
rows.note: The report describes a sweep/family, not a single checkpoint. Parity at approximately 4.2e26 FLOPs is an extrapolation, not an evaluated run.
rows.check: MDM byte and MDM BPE BPB both decline with compute, and the minima are fit to a power law (Fig 3 top). The persistent byte offset is not a V1 failure. V5 link removed (text pretraining, no new modality).

rows.subject: AR byte versus AR BPE model sweeps
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to byte/BPE BPB ratio as a function of compute.
rows.value: At BPB = 1.0, the reported compute gap is approximately 7.9× (2.3e20 for byte versus 2.9e19 for BPE); at BPB = 0.8, approximately 2.3× (2.7e21 versus 1.2e21).
rows.note: The paper says the ratio is fit to a power law and that the byte penalty decays faster for AR than for MDM.
rows.check: The byte/BPE ratio power law shows that slopes differ by representation. This bears on setup-dependence of exponents (V7), not on V5.

rows.subject: MDM byte versus MDM BPE model sweeps
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to byte/BPE BPB ratio as a function of compute.
rows.value: At BPB = 1.2, the reported compute gap is approximately 34.3× (1.2e21 for byte versus 3.5e19 for BPE); at BPB = 1.0, the projected gap is approximately 20.5× (9.0e21 versus 4.4e20).
rows.note: The paper says the ratio is fit to a power law; the BPB = 1.0 gap is a scaling projection.
rows.check: The MDM ratio fit decays more slowly than AR's, so the exponent depends on objective and representation (V7). The BPB=1.0 gap is a projection.

relationships.condition: AR and MDM, byte and BPE, Transformer, SlimPajama, 6e18–2e21 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Held-out BPB declines with compute in all four configurations, and isoFLOP minima fit a power law (Fig 3 top); S1, S2.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out bits per byte decreases with compute in all four configurations, and fixed-compute loss minima fit a power law.

relationships.reason: All seven tasks and the average rise (41.71→44.23); D33–D40.
relationships.display_finding: All seven task scores increased, with the average rising from 41.71 to 44.23.

relationships.reason: The average falls 37.73→36.76, BoolQ drops 60.64→44.86 and RACE is flat, although BPB improves with scale. Authors say there is no meaningful scaling. D42, D46, D48; other tasks rise slightly.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing size from 180M to 717M on 188B bytes improved BPB, but average performance fell from 37.73 to 36.76 and BoolQ from 60.64 to 44.86, while RACE remained flat and other tasks improved slightly.

relationships.condition: Byte vs BPE representation under AR vs MDM objectives
relationships.reason: Fitted BPB-vs-compute slopes differ by representation and objective. The byte/BPE ratio decays at objective-dependent rates; S3, S4.
relationships.display_finding: Bits-per-byte compute slopes varied with representation and objective, and the byte/BPE ratio decayed at objective-dependent rates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported AR and MDM text-pretraining compute sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The study reports declining BPB with compute and fits power-law relationships to scaling quantities; S1–S4 document the trajectories and fitted ratio results.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Byte versus BPE, especially masked diffusion
reader_labels.reason: The byte/BPE penalty behaves differently by objective and remains substantial for MDM across the studied range, so the result is not a single objective- and representation-independent trajectory; see S1–S4.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Text pretraining with AR versus masked-diffusion objectives
reader_labels.reason: The reported scaling overhead differs by objective: AR byte approaches BPE more quickly, while MDM byte retains a large offset; see S1–S4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: All seven listed task scores and their reported average are higher for the 717M AR byte model than for the 180M compute-matched AR byte model; see D33–D40.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Some task scores rise and others fall; the reported average declines from 37.73 to 36.76, consistent with the authors’ statement that this comparison does not show meaningful scaling; see D41–D48.
